extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and practitioners of scientific method and experimental inquiry (empirical scientists, methodologists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for performing and evaluating inductive reasoning and experimental inquiry in the sciences, with emphasis on the four methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Deduction) and complications introduced by multiple causes and mixed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify an antecedent A common to many instances in which effect a occurs (instances A B C → a, A D E → a) and infer a connection between A and a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only as a suggestive method unless instances are very numerous and widely varied; vulnerable to the characteristic imperfection that the same effect may have multiple causes (plurality of causes). The method can raise a strong presumption only after many varied instances all agreeing in A, or when followed up by experiments appealing to the Method of Difference. Anti-pattern: drawing firm causal conclusions from only two or a few agreeing instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare a positive instance (B C → b c) and a corresponding instance with an added antecedent (A B C → a b c); if adding A produces a, then A is either the cause of a or an indispensable part of its cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides rigorous and conclusive induction where applicable; only two instances (one positive, one negative) can suffice for a complete induction. Prefer this method whenever you can obtain (or simulate) paired instances that differ only by the presence/absence of the candidate antecedent. Example: experimental control where variable A is introduced/removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Indirect Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine the Method of Agreement (instances in which a is present all contain A) with the Method of Difference (instances in which a is absent all lack A) so that A is the only antecedent consistently present when a occurs and absent when a does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This joint method avoids the characteristic imperfection of the simple Method of Agreement and is very powerful—especially in observational sciences where direct experiments are limited. It effectively shows A to be not only a cause but the only possible cause. Use negative and positive premises together; obtain instances where the phenomenon is both present and absent and check consistent association with A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for Plurality of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the same effect may sometimes be produced by different causes (a may follow from A in one case, B in another); plurality of causes makes simple agreement-based inference uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a unique cause for an observed effect. Where plurality is possible, either (a) seek separate sets of instances to show different causal sequences, (b) multiply and vary instances to show one antecedent always present, or (c) accept several antecedents provisionally as distinct causes. Analysis (not mere counting) of instances is required. Anti-pattern: assuming causation from coincident antecedents without excluding alternate causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Negative Instances (absence-cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances in which the phenomenon does not occur (negative instances) are especially informative, because agreement among negative instances about the absence of A can exempt plurality-of-causes objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with negative as well as positive instances to apply the Joint Method; however, exhausting the field of negation is often practically infeasible (e.g., identifying what all non-transparent substances share). Use negatives when accessible and pair them with positives to strengthen causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary instances rather than increase sheer number
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplying instances that differ only in immaterial respects adds nothing to evidence; what matters is varying circumstances so that the only common antecedent left is the candidate cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single instance that eliminates a previously common antecedent is often more valuable than many similar repeats. First assure factual accuracy by repeating identical experiments; once assured, prioritize variation to exclude alternative antecedents. Anti-pattern: relying on massed repetition of the same kind of instance to justify causal certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use deduction to resolve intermixture of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When causes and effects are intermixed or interfere (composition of causes), direct inductive methods are often inadequate; deduction is required to unravel complexities and deduce constituent relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the four inductive methods primarily as ways of supplying premises and verifying deductions. In complex cases where individual effects are disguised or summed, form theoretical/deductive models that explain how component laws combine, then test their predictions empirically. Anti-pattern: expecting straightforward experimental separation of highly compounded effects without theoretical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect effects to be compounded and possibly disguised (Composition of Causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent causes often produce effects that are compounded (e.g., +a, -a, ½b) so that separate component effects are disguised in the observed result; the observed total may show no obvious relation to individual causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume absence of a law from lack of obvious instances; instead consider tendencies and concealed component effects. Use vector-like reasoning (sum of effects) and think in terms of tendencies, equilibrium, and compensation when analyzing such cases. Example: two equal and opposite forces producing rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express laws as tendencies rather than absolute outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because causes can be counteracted, statements of natural laws should say that an object 'tends' to behave in a way or experiences a 'tendency' toward an effect, not that the effect always actually occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt terminology reflecting tendencies (pressure, tendency to move) or qualify laws with 'unless prevented' / 'except so far as prevented.' This avoids the mistaken impression that laws have exceptions and clarifies that concurrent laws can act in all cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize chemical transformation and analysis as a methodological exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When combination produces a heteropathic effect that reproduces its causes (e.g., water yielding hydrogen and oxygen), chemical analysis can discover causes among effects because the compound can regenerate components under some conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where transformation allows reconstitution of original agents, experimental decomposition (analysis) yields direct evidence of constituents and the causes. But many heteropathic (chemical-like) effects in other domains (e.g., mental compounds) do not permit reconstitution and require synthetic study of components instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific experiments required for combined causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of separate agents’ laws often does not permit deductive inference about their combined effect; a specific experiment on the combination is usually necessary (e.g., hydrogen + oxygen → water requires experimenting on the mixture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and perform experiments that replicate the specific conjunction of antecedents suspected to produce the effect. Do not infer combinatory outcomes solely from separate-agent behavior; plan combinatory trials or seek natural instances where the combination occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid labeling co-acting principles as 'exceptions'
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent exceptions to a law are usually distinct concurrent principles that act together; there are not a law and an exception but multiple laws each acting in all cases with varying relative effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with an apparent exception, search for another concurrent cause modifying the first law instead of calling it an exception. Recast laws to reflect multiple concurrent tendencies so that 'exception' becomes recognition of another acting principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive proof requires active attempts to disprove hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses must end by being proved and are in reality proved by the Four Methods; merely collating facts consistent with a hypothesis without seeking disproof is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be content when a hypothesis remains undisproved by available facts; actively seek negative instances, perform Difference-method experiments, or derive deductive consequences that can be tested. Anti-pattern: accepting a hypothesis because no inconsistent fact is yet known (passive confirmation).
